claim: Macrophages undergo programmatic changes with age, leading to altered cytokine polarization and immune dysfunction.
source: Macrophages undergo programmatic changes with age, leading to altered cytokine polarization and immune dysfunction, shifting these critical immune cells from protective sentinels to disease promoters.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific understanding of macrophage aging.

claim: Mir146b expression progressively and unidirectionally declined with age in thioglycollate-elicited murine macrophages.
source: Using an unbiased RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) approach, we identified Mir146b as a microRNA whose expression progressively and unidirectionally declined with age in thioglycollate-elicited murine macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript showing Mir146b expression across different ages.

claim: Mir146b deficiency led to altered macrophage cytokine expression.
source: Mir146b deficiency led to altered macrophage cytokine expression and reduced mitochondrial metabolic activity, two hallmarks of cellular aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Mir146b knockout and knockdown experiments showing changes in cytokine gene expression.

claim: Mir146b deficiency led to reduced mitochondrial metabolic activity.
source: Mir146b deficiency led to altered macrophage cytokine expression and reduced mitochondrial metabolic activity, two hallmarks of cellular aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT assays, Seahorse metabolic measurements, and electron microscopy data showing mitochondrial dysfunction.

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq identified patterns of altered inflammation and interferon gamma signaling in Mir146b-deficient macrophages.
source: Single-cell RNA-seq identified patterns of altered inflammation and interferon gamma signaling in Mir146b-deficient macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing differential gene expression patterns in Mir146b-deficient cells.

claim: Macrophages perform critical surveillance functions and phagocytose pathogens and cellular debris.
source: Macrophages are innate immune cells that perform critical surveillance functions and phagocytose pathogens and cellular debris (Mosser and Edwards, 2008; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Macrophages signal to other cells and regulate diverse processes such as angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis through surface-bound or secreted factors.
source: Through surface-bound or secreted factors, they signal to other cells and regulate diverse processes such as angiogenesis, inflammation, and fibrosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about macrophage function.

claim: Macrophages are critical in regulating the molecular pathogenesis of cardiovascular disease, cancer, neurodegenerative disorders of the central nervous system, and blinding eye conditions.
source: These global functional consequences of macrophage activity make these cells critical in regulating the molecular pathogenesis of cardiovascular disease, cancer, neurodegenerative disorders of the central nervous system, and blinding eye conditions (Apte et al., 2006; Kelly et al., 2007; Nakao et al., 2005; Moore and Tabas, 2011; Mammana et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Macrophages undergo broad programmatic changes with aging that manifest as abnormal macrophage activation and polarization.
source: Macrophages undergo broad programmatic changes with aging that manifest as abnormal macrophage activation and polarization and are phenotypically labeled as immunosenescence or inflammaging (Xia et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2018; Sene and Apte, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Age-associated shift in macrophage phenotype occurs from disease protective to disease promoting.
source: This age-associated shift in the macrophage phenotype from disease protective to disease promoting led us to hypothesize that alterations in the aged macrophage transcriptome may regulate this dysfunction.
evidence: This claim is based on prior knowledge and citations, and serves as the rationale for the study hypothesis.

claim: Altered macrophage polarization and activation are associated with aging and drive molecular inflammation.
source: Altered macrophage polarization and activation are associated with aging and drive molecular inflammation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of macrophage aging.

claim: MicroRNAs regulate gene expression by either transcript degradation or translational repression.
source: Over the past decade, numerous studies have described how microRNAs (miRNAs), short non-coding RNAs ~22 nucleotides long, regulate gene expression by either transcript degradation or translational repression (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs approximately 22 nucleotides long.
source: Over the past decade, numerous studies have described how microRNAs (miRNAs), short non-coding RNAs ~22 nucleotides long, regulate gene expression by either transcript degradation or translational repression (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA structure.

claim: MiRNAs control critical processes in macrophages, including cholesterol efflux, lipid metabolism, and polarization.
source: Multiple laboratories have demonstrated that miRNAs control critical processes in macrophages, including cholesterol efflux, lipid metabolism, and polarization (Lin et al., 2018; Sene et al., 2013; Banerjee et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Expression of Mir146b progressively declines in the aging TGEM.
source: Here we demonstrate that expression of Mir146b progressively declines in the aging TGEM and is associated with significant mitochondrial dysfunction and abnormal macrophage activation and polarization, recapitulating the inflammaging phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data showing declining Mir146b expression with age.

claim: Declining Mir146b expression is associated with significant mitochondrial dysfunction in TGEMs.
source: Here we demonstrate that expression of Mir146b progressively declines in the aging TGEM and is associated with significant mitochondrial dysfunction and abnormal macrophage activation and polarization, recapitulating the inflammaging phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy, MTT assays, and Seahorse metabolic measurements.

claim: Declining Mir146b expression is associated with abnormal macrophage activation and polarization.
source: Here we demonstrate that expression of Mir146b progressively declines in the aging TGEM and is associated with significant mitochondrial dysfunction and abnormal macrophage activation and polarization, recapitulating the inflammaging phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine gene expression data from knockout and knockdown experiments.

claim: Approximately 95% of cells collected by the TGEM isolation method stained double-positive for CD11b and F4/80 macrophage markers.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed that approximately 95% of all cells stained double-positive for both markers, confirming these cells as macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The age of the mouse from which TGEMs were harvested does not impact the purity of the TGEM population.
source: Moreover, we confirmed that the age of the mouse from which the cells were harvested does not impact the purity of the TGEM population obtained through this procedure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing young and old mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mir146b expression decreased more than twofold in TGEMs isolated from 3-month-old vs 30-month-old female mice.
source: We indeed observed a decrease of more than twofold in Mir146b gene expression in TGEMs isolated from 3-month-old vs 30-month-old female mice (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Levels of Mir146b declined with age in BMDMs.
source: Levels of Mir146b also declined with age in BMDMs (Figure 1C)
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mir146b relative expression in unstimulated BMDMs from individual 3-month-old female mice was only approximately 20% of that in TGEMs.
source: however, Mir146b relative expression in unstimulated BMDMs from individual 3-month-old female mice was only ~20% of that in TGEMs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data comparing TGEMs and BMDMs shown in Figure 1D.

claim: QuantiGene 2.0 miRNA plate assay confirmed a comparable decrease in Mir146b relative expression levels from 3 to 30 months in TGEMs.
source: Here we further confirmed a comparable decrease in Mir146b relative expression levels from 3 to 30 months in TGEMs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by QuantiGene assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mir146b expression was below the limit of detection in naive BMDMs from both young and old female mice using the QuantiGene assay.
source: Expression was below the limit of detection in naive BMDMs (data not shown) from both young and old female mice.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data that was not shown in the manuscript.

claim: Small RNAs such as miRNAs primarily regulate gene silencing within cells by binding to canonical target seed sequences in the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of protein coding genes to initiate a process of post-transcriptional degradation.
source: Small RNAs such as miRNAs primarily regulate gene silencing within cells by binding to canonical target seed sequences in the 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of protein coding genes to initiate a process of post-transcriptional degradation (Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Age causes poorly understood programmatic changes within the macrophage that lead to a shift in polarization that promotes dysfunctional immunity and disease.
source: Age causes poorly understood programmatic changes within the macrophage that lead to a shift in polarization that promotes dysfunctional immunity and disease (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mir146b showed a consistent unidirectional alteration in expression pattern over the lifetime of a mouse.
source: RNA-seq and subsequent qPCR validation demonstrated that Mir146b showed a consistent unidirectional alteration in expression pattern over the lifetime of a mouse.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transfection efficiency of TGEMs with Mir146b inhibitor was approximately 80%.
source: We measured the transfection efficiency (in separate wells) using a fluorescently tagged sham inhibitor of similar nucleotide length and noted a transfection efficiency of approximately 80%, with less than 2% cell death assessed by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) (Figure 2A and data not shown) 24 hr post-transfection.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transfection of TGEMs with Mir146b inhibitor resulted in less than 2% cell death assessed by TUNEL 24 hr post-transfection.
source: We measured the transfection efficiency (in separate wells) using a fluorescently tagged sham inhibitor of similar nucleotide length and noted a transfection efficiency of approximately 80%, with less than 2% cell death assessed by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling (TUNEL) (Figure 2A and data not shown) 24 hr post-transfection.
evidence: This claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The transfection protocol resulted in greater than 50% reduction in macrophage Mir146b miRNA expression levels when measured by qPCR.
source: This transfection protocol resulted in >50% reduction in macrophage Mir146b miRNA expression levels when measured by qPCR (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Knockdown of Mir146b for 72 hr in TGEMs resulted in trends of decreased gene expression of multiple cytokines and regulatory markers including Nos2, Mmp9, Il1b, Il6, Arg1, and Cd163.
source: Knockdown of Mir146b for 72 hr in TGEMs resulted in trends of decreased gene expression of multiple cytokines and regulatory markers including Nos2, Mmp9, Il1b, Il6, Arg1, and Cd163 along with a trend toward increased Il10 (Figure 2C) when compared to the relative expression in sham-transfected control TGEMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Knockdown of Mir146b for 72 hr in TGEMs resulted in a trend toward increased Il10.
source: Knockdown of Mir146b for 72 hr in TGEMs resulted in trends of decreased gene expression of multiple cytokines and regulatory markers including Nos2, Mmp9, Il1b, Il6, Arg1, and Cd163 along with a trend toward increased Il10 (Figure 2C) when compared to the relative expression in sham-transfected control TGEMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mir146b knockdown results phenocopy aging macrophage phenotypes previously reported of decreasing M1-associated cytokine markers with simultaneously elevated Il10.
source: These results implicate Mir146b in regulating genes associated with macrophage polarization and inflammation, phenocopying aging macrophage phenotypes previously reported by our lab and others of decreasing M1-associated cytokine markers with simultaneously elevated Il10 (Kelly et al., 2007; Sene et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: TGEMs from young female cKO mice have significantly reduced Mir146b gene expression levels compared to TGEMs from female littermate Controls.
source: Mir146b loss was confirmed by qPCR using independent biological replicates from 3-month-old females (Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was no compensation in expression of the Mir146 family member Mir146a in Mir146b cKO mice.
source: and we determined that there was no compensation in expression of the Mir146 family member Mir146a (Figure 2E), whose mature sequence differs by only two nucleotides, both located outside of the seed region.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The mature sequence of Mir146a differs from Mir146b by only two nucleotides, both located outside of the seed region.
source: and we determined that there was no compensation in expression of the Mir146 family member Mir146a (Figure 2E), whose mature sequence differs by only two nucleotides, both located outside of the seed region.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sequence similarity between Mir146a and Mir146b.

claim: TGEMs harvested from young female cKO mice displayed altered polarization on gene expression analysis similar to that observed with Mir146b knockdown in TGEMs.
source: TGEMs harvested from young (6–12 weeks old) female cKO mice displayed altered polarization on gene expression analysis (Figure 2F) similar to that observed with Mir146b knockdown in TGEMs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 2F and comparison to Figure 2C.

claim: Compared to TGEMs isolated from littermate Controls, cKO TGEMs expressed lower levels of Nos2, Il1b, Il6, and Ccl2.
source: Compared to TGEMs isolated from littermate Controls, cKO TGEMs expressed lower levels of Nos2, Il1b, Il6, and Ccl2, traditionally associated with classical macrophage polarization, as well as Arg1 and Cd163.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: cKO TGEMs expressed lower levels of Arg1 and Cd163 compared to littermate Controls.
source: Compared to TGEMs isolated from littermate Controls, cKO TGEMs expressed lower levels of Nos2, Il1b, Il6, and Ccl2, traditionally associated with classical macrophage polarization, as well as Arg1 and Cd163.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: cKO TGEMs displayed a trend toward increased expression of Il10 compared to littermate Controls.
source: They also displayed a trend toward increased expression of the cytokine associated with alternative activation, Il10, all similar to the pattern observed following in vitro knockdown of Mir146b.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mmp9 showed an increasing trend in cKO TGEMs compared to littermate Controls.
source: However, Mmp9, which decreased following knockdown, showed an increasing trend in cKO TGEMs compared to littermate Controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR gene expression data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TGEMs from cKO female mice had a decreased number of mitochondria compared to littermate Controls.
source: Analysis revealed a decreased number of mitochondria in TGEMs lacking Mir146b compared to littermate Controls (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Mitochondria from cKO macrophages had increased intercrystal spaces (ICS) compared to Control TGEMs.
source: In addition, the mitochondria from cKO macrophages had increased intercrystal spaces (ICS) compared to Control TGEMs (Figure 3D–F), which may affect mitochondrial respiration and metabolic function.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Increased intercrystal spaces in mitochondria may affect mitochondrial respiration and metabolic function.
source: In addition, the mitochondria from cKO macrophages had increased intercrystal spaces (ICS) compared to Control TGEMs (Figure 3D–F), which may affect mitochondrial respiration and metabolic function.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed structural changes.

claim: TGEMs from young female cKO mice reduce less MTT compared to Control macrophages, indicating decreased metabolic activity.
source: Compared to Control macrophages under standard tissue culture conditions, TGEMs from young female cKO mice reduce less MTT, indicating decreased metabolic activity (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: cKO TGEMs displayed a significant decline in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) maximal respiration after treatment with FCCP.
source: cKO TGEMs displayed a significant decline in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) maximal respiration, as assessed after treatment with the uncoupling agent carbonyl cyanide 4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone (FCCP) (Figure 3H)
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF MitoStress assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: cKO TGEMs displayed decreased extracellular acidification rates (ECARs).
source: as well as decreased extracellular acidification rates (ECARs) (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF MitoStress assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Macrophages lacking Mir146b have decreased metabolic activity.
source: Together, these results indicate that macrophages lacking Mir146b have decreased metabolic activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the MTT and Seahorse data.

claim: Overexpression of Mir146b mimic for 48 hr in TGEMs from young C57Bl/6J wildtype mice increased maximal mitochondrial respiration (OCR) rates compared to scramble-transfected controls.
source: Interestingly, when we overexpressed Mir146b mimic for 48 hr by transient transfection in TGEMs from young C57Bl/6J wildtype mice, the maximal mitochondrial respiration (OCR) rates and ECAR were increased compared to scramble-transfected controls (Figure 3J–K)
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF MitoStress assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Overexpression of Mir146b mimic for 48 hr in TGEMs from young C57Bl/6J wildtype mice increased ECAR compared to scramble-transfected controls.
source: Interestingly, when we overexpressed Mir146b mimic for 48 hr by transient transfection in TGEMs from young C57Bl/6J wildtype mice, the maximal mitochondrial respiration (OCR) rates and ECAR were increased compared to scramble-transfected controls (Figure 3J–K)
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse XF MitoStress assay data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Mir146b levels influence gene expression and mitochondrial function in TGEMs.
source: providing further evidence that Mir146b levels influence gene expression and mitochondrial function in TGEMs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the overexpression data.

claim: Several genes significantly downregulated in Mir146b cKO TGEMs have critical roles in both mitochondrial morphology and respiration.
source: We found several genes significantly downregulated in Mir146b cKO TGEMs, which have critical roles in both mitochondrial morphology and respiration (Sdhd, Crtc2, Pnpt1, Gdf15, Mrps28, Mterf3, Med30 Rnaseh1, Slc19a2, and Gtpbp10) (Gottlieb and Tomlinson, 2005; Linke et al., 2017; Shimada et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019; Sylvester et al., 2004; Taylor and Turnbull, 2007; Krebs et al., 2011; Lima et al., 2016; Jungtrakoon et al., 2019; Lavdovskaia et al., 2018; Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A and citations to prior literature about these genes.

claim: Macrophage Mir146b deficiency affects genes in the macrophage transcriptome that broadly regulate mitochondrial function and metabolism.
source: These findings suggest that macrophage Mir146b deficiency affects genes in the macrophage transcriptome that broadly regulate mitochondrial function and metabolism, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and reduced metabolic capacity, similar to what is seen with aging (Xia et al., 2016; van Beek et al., 2019; Pence and Yarbro, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data and comparison to prior literature on aging.

claim: Only one gene, Lyz1, demonstrated a statistically significant increase in expression upon the loss of Mir146b in TGEMs.
source: Interestingly, only one gene, Lyz1, demonstrated a statistically significant increase in expression upon the loss of Mir146b in TGEMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lyz1 is a macrophage marker that has not previously been associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Lyz1 is a macrophage marker that has not previously been associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, and these results could not be replicated in mir146b overexpression experiments, where levels of Lyz1 were unaffected (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Lyz1 and experimental data from overexpression experiments.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis revealed three transcriptionally distinct clusters of TGEMs.
source: Analysis revealed three transcriptionally distinct clusters (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All three clusters of TGEMs expressed macrophage markers including Mertk, Csf1r, and Cd68.
source: All clusters expressed macrophage markers including Mertk, Csf1r, and Cd68 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of markers including Apoe, Ms4a7, H2-DMa, C3, and Cd74 was enriched in Cluster 1, indicating that these cells represent mature recruited monocyte-derived macrophages specialized for antigen presentation.
source: Expression of markers including Apoe, Ms4a7, H2-DMa, C3, and Cd74 was enriched in Cluster 1, indicating that these cells represent mature recruited monocyte-derived macrophages specialized for antigen presentation.
evidence: This claim is based on single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D and inference from marker expression patterns.

claim: Canonical biomarkers of resident peritoneal macrophages Gata6, Vsig4, Timd4, and Marco were enriched in Cluster 2 cells.
source: Meanwhile, canonical biomarkers of resident peritoneal macrophages Gata6, Vsig4, Timd4, and Marco were enriched in Cluster 2 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cluster 3 cells showed elevated expression of genes corresponding to highly active recruited macrophages including Atp6v0d2, Htra1, Mfge8, and Chpt1.
source: Resident macrophage markers were virtually absent from Cluster 3, but these cells showed elevated expression of genes corresponding to highly active recruited macrophages including Atp6v0d2, Htra1, Mfge8, and Chpt1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A majority of the down-regulated genes identified by bulk RNA-seq displayed lower expression in clusters 1 and 3 of cells from cKO mice.
source: A majority of the down-regulated genes identified by bulk RNA-seq displayed lower expression in clusters 1 and 3 of cells from cKO mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The loss of expression of downregulated genes is consistent with a premature aging phenotype as many of the genes also show decreased expression in aged Control macrophages compared to young Control cells.
source: This loss of expression is consistent with a premature aging phenotype as many of the genes also show decreased expression in aged Control macrophages compared to young Control cells, although the resident peritoneal macrophages (Cluster 2) displayed equal or elevated expression of a subset of the genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of gene expression patterns across age and genotype in the single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: Lyz1 was most highly expressed in resident peritoneal macrophages (Cluster 2).
source: Lyz1, which was upregulated in cKO TGEMs in the bulk RNA-seq, was most highly expressed in resident peritoneal macrophages (Cluster 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Lyz1 expression increased in cKO macrophages across all clusters compared to the Control counterparts.
source: Its expression increased in cKO macrophages across all clusters compared to the Control counterparts; however, this increase was not recapitulated by natural aging (young Control vs old Control).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The increase in Lyz1 expression in cKO macrophages was not recapitulated by natural aging.
source: Its expression increased in cKO macrophages across all clusters compared to the Control counterparts; however, this increase was not recapitulated by natural aging (young Control vs old Control).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The majority of cells from all genotypes belonged to Cluster 1.
source: Since the majority of cells belonged to Cluster 1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), we hypothesized that transcriptional differences amongst this population of cells would likely have contributed most to the observed mitochondrial dysfunction of Mir146b conditional knockout TGEMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Five hierarchically defined expression patterns were identified amongst Cluster 1 cells between the four samples (young Control, young cKO, old Control, and old cKO).
source: We analyzed differential gene expression of Cluster 1 cells between the four samples (young Control, young cKO, old Control, and old cKO) and identified five (a–e) hierarchically defined expression patterns amongst our four groups (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Four out of five expression patterns showed loss of gene expression in old cKO macrophages compared to age-matched controls (patterns b–e).
source: As with our bulk RNA-seq, we again primarily noted decreases in gene expression, with four out of five patterns showing loss of gene expression in old cKO macrophages compared to age-matched controls (patterns b–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Genes within pattern b were enriched for cellular functions such as cholesterol transport and biosynthesis.
source: Genes within these patterns were enriched for cellular functions such as cholesterol transport and biosynthesis (pattern b), scavenging/phagocytosis and migration (pattern c), negative regulation of inflammation (pattern d), and calcium homeostasis and endocytosis (pattern e).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene ontology or pathway analysis of the genes in pattern b.

claim: Genes within pattern c were enriched for scavenging/phagocytosis and migration.
source: Genes within these patterns were enriched for cellular functions such as cholesterol transport and biosynthesis (pattern b), scavenging/phagocytosis and migration (pattern c), negative regulation of inflammation (pattern d), and calcium homeostasis and endocytosis (pattern e).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene ontology or pathway analysis of the genes in pattern c.

claim: Genes within pattern d were enriched for negative regulation of inflammation.
source: Genes within these patterns were enriched for cellular functions such as cholesterol transport and biosynthesis (pattern b), scavenging/phagocytosis and migration (pattern c), negative regulation of inflammation (pattern d), and calcium homeostasis and endocytosis (pattern e).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene ontology or pathway analysis of the genes in pattern d.

claim: Genes within pattern e were enriched for calcium homeostasis and endocytosis.
source: Genes within these patterns were enriched for cellular functions such as cholesterol transport and biosynthesis (pattern b), scavenging/phagocytosis and migration (pattern c), negative regulation of inflammation (pattern d), and calcium homeostasis and endocytosis (pattern e).
evidence: This is an inference based on gene ontology or pathway analysis of the genes in pattern e.

claim: Pattern a highlighted genes that normally show only small decreases with age but were significantly increased in aged cKO TGEMs.
source: Pattern a, however, highlighted genes that normally show only small decreases with age but were significantly increased in aged cKO TGEMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Of the 28 genes differentially expressed in pattern a, six are integral to the interferon gamma (IFNy) signaling pathway.
source: Interestingly, of the 28 genes differentially expressed in pattern a, six are integral to the interferon gamma (IFNy) signaling pathway, including interferon-stimulated gene 15 (Isg15), C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 (Ccl5), interferon-induced transmembrane 3 (Ifitm3), interferon regulatory factor 7 (Irf7), interleukin-18 binding protein (Il18bp), and secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor (Slpi).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the genes in pattern a and their known roles in IFNy signaling.

claim: IFNy treatment has been demonstrated to significantly reduce the respiratory capacity of macrophages in culture.
source: These findings are especially informative as IFNy treatment has been demonstrated to significantly reduce the respiratory capacity of macrophages in culture (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A loss of Mir146b in TGEMs may contribute to abnormal activation, polarization, mitochondrial dysfunction, and parainflammation as seen with macrophage aging.
source: These data further demonstrate that a loss of Mir146b in TGEMs may contribute to abnormal activation, polarization, mitochondrial dysfunction, and parainflammation as seen with macrophage aging.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the combined experimental data.

claim: Macrophage-mediated inflammation has been implicated in promoting dysfunctional immunity in many disorders of aging.
source: Macrophage-mediated inflammation has been implicated in promoting dysfunctional immunity in many of these disorders of aging; however, the molecular mechanisms by which aging leads to dysregulated macrophage function remain unknown.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The molecular mechanisms by which aging leads to dysregulated macrophage function remain unknown.
source: Macrophage-mediated inflammation has been implicated in promoting dysfunctional immunity in many of these disorders of aging; however, the molecular mechanisms by which aging leads to dysregulated macrophage function remain unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Programmatic alteration of macrophage gene expression (coding transcriptome) with age precedes the downstream effects on macrophage proteome and function.
source: Programmatic alteration of macrophage gene expression (coding transcriptome) with age precedes the downstream effects on macrophage proteome and function.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the central dogma of molecular biology.

claim: Mir146b and Mir22 were identified as microRNAs whose expression progressively decrease with age in TGEMs from female mice.
source: We identified Mir146b and Mir22 as microRNAs whose expression progressively decrease with age in TGEMs from female mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and qPCR validation data.

claim: Mir146b expression was noted to be greater than 3.3-fold higher in macrophages from young (3 months old) mice compared to Mir22.
source: Mir146b expression was noted to be greater than 3.3-fold higher in macrophages from young (3 months old) mice compared to Mir22.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Mir146b expression significantly decreases from 3 to 30 months in not only TGEMs but also BMDMs.
source: Regardless, our subsequent qPCR data confirm that Mir146b expression significantly decreases from 3 to 30 months in not only TGEMs but also BMDMs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Loss of Mir146b in TGEMs resulted in altered cytokine expression and polarization that parallels low-grade chronic inflammation associated with aging.
source: Loss of Mir146b in TGEMs, established by both the transient knockdown ex vivo and a novel conditional macrophage/monocyte knockout mouse, resulted in altered cytokine expression and polarization that parallels low-grade chronic inflammation associated with aging (van Beek et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine gene expression data and comparison to prior literature on aging.

claim: Mir146b deletion in TGEMs results in an abnormal mitochondrial structure.
source: We demonstrated that Mir146b deletion in TGEMs results in an abnormal mitochondrial structure and dysfunctional mitochondrial metabolism, characterized by a decreased OCR and ECAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data showing structural abnormalities.

claim: Mir146b deletion in TGEMs results in dysfunctional mitochondrial metabolism, characterized by a decreased OCR and ECAR.
source: We demonstrated that Mir146b deletion in TGEMs results in an abnormal mitochondrial structure and dysfunctional mitochondrial metabolism, characterized by a decreased OCR and ECAR.
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse metabolic measurements.

claim: The mitochondrial dysfunction phenotype was reversed with Mir146b overexpression.
source: Interestingly, this phenotype was reversed with Mir146b overexpression.
evidence: This claim is supported by Seahorse data from Mir146b overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3J-K.

claim: Altered gene expression of multiple mitochondria-related genes was identified in TGEMs deficient in Mir146b utilizing RNA-seq.
source: Perhaps, not surprisingly, given our observed TEM and Seahorse findings, we identified altered gene expression of multiple mitochondria-related genes as well as genes critical to glucose metabolism in TGEMs deficient in Mir146b utilizing RNA-seq.
evidence: This claim is supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Age-related reductions in oxidative phosphorylation have been noted in macrophages.
source: Age-related reductions in oxidative phosphorylation have been noted not only in macrophages (Lin et al., 2018) but also in myriad cell types, including cardiomyocytes (Lesnefsky et al., 2016; Tepp et al., 2017), intestinal mucosal epithelial cells (Özsoy et al., 2020), and retinal pigment epithelium of AMD patients compared to age-matched healthy controls (Ferrington et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Age-related reductions in oxidative phosphorylation may serve as an important indicator of age-related disease and progression.
